articles.title: Your GPU Is Nerfed for AI How Do You Unlock It?
articles.author: Codacus
articles.summary: Unlock your GPU, and have a 2x speed up for local ai on rtx cards with llamacpp and strata. NVIDIA's own spec sheets list FP16 and BF16 matrix math with FP32 accumulate at half speed on every GeForce RTX card since the 2080 Ti, while the workstation cards built on the same chip run it at full speed.
articles.content:
Unlock your GPU, and have a 2x speed up for local ai on rtx cards with llamacpp and strata.
NVIDIA's own spec sheets list FP16 and BF16 matrix math with FP32 accumulate at half speed on every GeForce RTX card since the 2080 Ti, while the workstation cards built on the same chip run it at full speed. The community found a way to switch it back to full speed on Linux, using a bug in NVIDIA's own boot firmware. Nothing gets flashed, and it resets when you power off.

I unlocked both RTX 3060s in my home server and measured what changed, from matrix math to llama.cpp, Strata and image generation, and which cards it works on.

Measured on my system (2x RTX 3060 12 GB, Linux):
- cuBLAS 8192 matrix multiply, FP16 inputs with FP32 total: 27.25 → 49.39 TFLOPS (+81%). BF16 +82%, TF32 +93%. Output identical before and after.
- llama.cpp (Qwen3-VL 8B Q8_0): prefill at 512 tokens 2176 → 2182 t/s, at 16k +4.6%, decode flat at 39.1 t/s.
- Strata (MoE engine), 32k-token prompt: prefill 812 → 950 t/s (+17%).

Source repos (build only from these; there is no ready-made Windows unlocker, and in 2022 a fake "LHR unlocker" for RTX 30 cards shipped with malware):
RTX 30 (Ampere): https://github.com/Zagitta/gpu-unlock
RTX 20 (Turing): https://github.com/nlzy/turing-unlock
RTX 40 (Ada, early fork): https://github.com/JustAResearcher/gpu-unlock-ada
The 3060 fix I needed (device 10de:2544): https://github.com/Zagitta/gpu-unlock/pull/35

NVIDIA whitepapers (find your card's row: FP16 Tensor TFLOPS with FP32 Accumulate):
Turing: https://images.nvidia.com/aem-dam/en-zz/Solutions/design-visualization/technologies/turing-architecture/NVIDIA-Turing-Architecture-Whitepaper.pdf
Ampere GA102: https://www.nvidia.com/content/PDF/nvidia-ampere-ga-102-gpu-architecture-whitepaper-v2.pdf
Ada: https://images.nvidia.com/aem-dam/Solutions/geforce/ada/nvidia-ada-gpu-architecture.pdf
Blackwell: https://images.nvidia.com/aem-dam/Solutions/geforce/blackwell/nvidia-rtx-blackwell-gpu-architecture.pdf

Other sources:
The 2018 fast.ai thread on half-speed FP32 accumulate: https://forums.fast.ai/t/geforce-rtx-half-speed-fp32-accumulate-in-mixed-prec-mode/33113
CMP 170HX mining card unlock (Tom's Hardware): https://www.tomshardware.com/pc-components/gpus/nvidia-crypto-mining-gpus-hacked-to-restore-locked-away-vram-in-order-to-feed-ai-boom-software-mod-unlocks-64gb-of-vram-on-usd250-cmp-170hx
Hacker News discussion: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50219700
Steam Hardware Survey: https://store.steampowered.com/hwsurvey/videocard/

Credit to Zagitta for gpu-unlock, and to Jon Pry, whose work on NVIDIA's mining cards it builds on.

Before you try it: a failed attempt can leave the card unusable until you power the machine off, and the code is new. Read the repo's README and issue tracker for your exact card first.

Tell me in the comments which card and which engine you run, and I'll tell you if it's worth it.

articles.title: Can Running AI in a Loop Make It Smarter on the Same GPU?
articles.author: Codacus
articles.summary: This video is sponsored by ego lite, a free browser for AI agents with open-source Skills. Try ego lite free: https://link.ego.app/Codacus Rumours say GPT-6.1 Sol is just GPT-6 Sol, looped twice. A looped transformer runs part of its layer stack again for every token, so the model spends more comput
articles.content:
This video is sponsored by ego lite, a free browser for AI agents with open-source Skills.
Try ego lite free: https://link.ego.app/Codacus

Rumours say GPT-6.1 Sol is just GPT-6 Sol, looped twice. A looped transformer runs part of its layer stack again for every token, so the model spends more compute on the same weights, on the same GPU. I tried to turn my own local models into looped transformers to see whether that actually makes them smarter, then ran NVIDIA's Dory, a 4B model trained to loop, on one RTX 3060.

What I found:
- Running four middle blocks of Qwen3-4B twice, the naive way, made it worse: MMLU-Pro dropped 8.35 points and CommonsenseQA 6.63.
- The training-free fix from the paper (a half step on the second pass) brought it back to about the base score. Every gain it gave me was small enough to be noise, and so was the best of 23 loop windows I tried on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (I had to patch llama.cpp so a second pass doesn't write into its linear-attention memory twice).
- A control test with no loop at all beat my loops: pasting the question twice raised MMLU-Pro by 3.5 points.
- With thinking on, looping the 35B fixed 8 answers and broke 9. Nothing I could count on.
- Dory, trained with the loop from the start, gets real gains from its second loop on NVIDIA's numbers: SWE-bench Verified 50.3 → 59.5. On my RTX 3060 at 8K context it runs at 52 / 35 / 21 tokens per second at 1 / 2 / 4 loops, and VRAM goes from 3.8 GB to 4.1 GB at two loops.
- Its knowledge score stays at 10 whether it loops once or four times. A loop adds compute to apply what a model knows. It does not add knowledge.

The test results are mine, from my own runs. Dory's benchmark scores are NVIDIA's. The GPT-6.1 Sol claims are rumours: The Information's report, a Microsoft model-card line that was removed within hours, and a LessWrong analysis. OpenAI has not confirmed any of it.

⏱️ CHAPTERS
0:00 Can running AI in a loop make it smarter?
0:31 Why is everyone looping? (the GPT-6.1 Sol rumour)
2:20 Sponsor: ego lite
3:53 How does a loop work?
5:23 What if I just run it twice?
6:58 How do you loop it safely?
9:44 Wait, just paste it twice?
12:09 Isn't that just thinking?
13:58 Just keep looping: NVIDIA's Dory on one RTX 3060
17:45 So, does it get smarter?

🧪 RUN DORY YOURSELF (llama.cpp)
Dory support is in NVIDIA's draft pull request, not in mainline llama.cpp yet.
1. Build llama.cpp from the PR branch: https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/30306 (branch dory-support; the model card pins commit 98a74c97ea09ac72f6ceda1559808fc0a2f447ce)
2. Download the GGUF (dory-q5_k_m.gguf, 3.67 GB): https://huggingface.co/nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-Labs-Dory1.0-4B-GGUF
3. Run it at two loops (the file defaults to four; the extra two mostly cost speed):
--override-kv "dory.num_loops=int:2,dory.recurrent_kv_cache_mode=str:per_loop" --flash-attn off

▶ Training-Free Looped Transformers (the paper I followed): https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.23872
▶ Prompt Repetition (pasting the question twice): https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.14982
▶ LessWrong, GPT-6.1 Sol nearly matches the no-CoT performance of GPT-6 Astra: https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/LqSZZAriGqgsGDQe3/gpt-6-1-sol-nearly-matches-the-no-cot-performance-of-gpt-6
▶ The Information, OpenAI Technique in 'Astra' Model Sparks Security Concerns: https://www.theinformation.com/articles/secret-technique-behind-openais-astra-model-sparks-security-concerns
▶ TechCrunch on the same report: https://techcrunch.com/2026/09/02/openais-new-reasoning-technique-alarms-ai-safety-experts/
▶ The Microsoft model-card screenshot (posted by @Algorithon): https://x.com/Algorithon/status/2107287650881208694

articles.title: Can a Local LLM Speak and Listen at the Same Time? | Full Duplex Voice AI
articles.author: Codacus
articles.summary: Full-duplex voice AI on a local LLM. A normal 35B text model (Qwen3.6-35B-A3B) listens while it talks, on a single RTX 3060 12GB with llama.cpp. There is no voice activity detection (VAD) in the loop and no new speech-to-speech model. This year Thinking Machines Lab showed its interaction model and
articles.content:
Full-duplex voice AI on a local LLM. A normal 35B text model (Qwen3.6-35B-A3B) listens while it talks, on a single RTX 3060 12GB with llama.cpp. There is no voice activity detection (VAD) in the loop and no new speech-to-speech model.

This year Thinking Machines Lab showed its interaction model and OpenAI launched GPT-Live, the new ChatGPT voice mode. Both are full duplex: the AI can speak and listen at the same time, so it reacts while you are still talking. Both labs trained a brand new model for it. This video gets that behaviour out of an open-weight text LLM you can run at home.

The trick is micro-turns. Every 0.6 seconds, speech-to-text hands the model the few words you just said, and the model either writes a few words for text-to-speech or stays silent. A CPU core runs two programs the same way: it does one thing at a time and switches fast enough that you stop noticing. The idea comes from the DuplexCascade paper (link below).

Prompting alone gets part of the way. The rest took LoRA fine-tuning on the last 4 layers of the 35B MoE: about 3 hours on two 12GB GPUs, on a few hundred synthetic conversations written by another LLM. The LoRA adapter is on Hugging Face, with a small client so you can try it with llama.cpp.

In the video:
- How GPT-Live, Thinking Machines and the open full-duplex speech models (Moshi, PersonaPlex) work, and why the classic voice assistant pipeline (VAD, speech-to-text, LLM, text-to-speech) has to take turns like a walkie-talkie
- The 0.6 s micro-turn loop: chopping your speech into slices and letting the LLM decide, slice by slice, whether to speak or listen
- Why a system prompt is not enough: a chat model is trained to always answer
- Fine-tuning a 35B on two RTX 3060s: caching the frozen layers and training a LoRA on the top four
- Five training runs and what each one broke: the model that would not stop talking, the fillers ("mm-hm") it overused, and the dataset bias behind both
- "73% sure": why it kept stopping three words into a sentence, and the decoding fix
- Three uncut demos of the real-time voice assistant: it says "mm-hm" while I talk, it waits through my thinking pauses, and it interrupts me to warn about mixing bleach and ammonia
- The scoreboard, including what it still gets wrong: about 3 seconds to its first word, hazards caught 6 times out of 10, fillers in the right spot about 1 time in 3

All numbers are from my own runs on my own machine, except the Moshi and VoiceBench figures, which are from the DuplexCascade paper.

▶ Base model (GGUF, Q4_K_M): https://huggingface.co/unsloth/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-GGUF

articles.title: This Engine Makes 177B Qwen 3.8 Flash Extremely Fast with 12GB GPU | Strata
articles.author: Codacus
articles.summary: A voice agent placed a real grocery order, start to finish, in under two minutes. The model behind it was Qwen 3.8 Flash, 177B parameters counting its n-gram tables, running on one RTX 3060 with 12GB of VRAM and 64GB of system RAM. The engine that made that possible is Strata, an open-source (MIT) i
articles.content:
A voice agent placed a real grocery order, start to finish, in under two minutes. The model behind it was Qwen 3.8 Flash, 177B parameters counting its n-gram tables, running on one RTX 3060 with 12GB of VRAM and 64GB of system RAM.

The engine that made that possible is Strata, an open-source (MIT) inference engine that is about two weeks old and runs exactly one model. llama.cpp supports around 150 architectures. Strata supports this one, and because it only has to fit one model's shapes, it can plan memory and scheduling around them.

The number that matters for agents is prompt processing, because an agent re-reads a long prompt on every call. In my shoping cart run the agent made 26 model calls and read about 20 tokens for every token it wrote. On the same card, my llama.cpp setup last month read prompts at about 120 tokens a second. Strata reads them at 900+. Generation is about 40 tokens a second.

In the video:
- What Strata is, and why a single-model engine can be this much faster
- How it reads prompts almost 8× faster: bigger chunks in borrowed VRAM, a streaming ring for the experts, and sparse attention without a giant mask. The expert matrix-multiply kernel is llama.cpp's own.
- Decode: a per-expert cache, the CPU and GPU working on the same layer, and multi-token prediction
- The setup: install on Windows or Linux, then run Strata and llama.cpp behind one endpoint with llama-swap, so every model is reachable by name
- What it costs: one model, one request at a time, about 40GB of pinned RAM, and a freeze on first start
- Can llama.cpp catch up? I ported the prefill ideas into my own fork and took it from about 120 to about 620 tokens a second in two days.
- The verdict: can it replace the 35B MoE as an everyday local model?

All numbers are from my own runs on my own machine.

⏱️ CHAPTERS

Most local AI setups struggle with massive models. I found an engine that makes Qwen 3.8 Flash run at 900 tokens per second.

Running a 177B model on a budget RTX 3060 shouldn't be possible, but the Strata inference engine changes the math. By focusing on a single architecture rather than broad compatibility, it optimizes memory scheduling to fit these huge parameters where they usually wouldn't go. It handles the heavy lifting on my 12GB card without requiring a server rack.

To see if the speed holds up in practice, I built an agent to complete a shopping task. It searched for items and finalized a transaction for toothpaste and a toothbrush in under two minutes. This local AI performance proves you can run sophisticated reasoning on consumer hardware if you use the right tools.

Subscribe for weekly hardware breakdowns, and let me know in the comments what tasks you would automate with this setup.

articles.title: Adding a Second GPU to My AI Rig: Does It Double the Speed?
articles.author: Codacus
articles.summary: I added a second RTX 3060 to my local AI server. Did it double the speed? The answer isn't one number: some models more than doubled, and AI video refused to use the second card at all until I changed how it runs. This is the full build and setup of AI Rig, my dual RTX 3060 AI server: the parts, the
articles.content:
I added a second RTX 3060 to my local AI server. Did it double the speed? The answer isn't one number: some models more than doubled, and AI video refused to use the second card at all until I changed how it runs.

This is the full build and setup of AI Rig, my dual RTX 3060 AI server: the parts, the motherboard mistake I made, Proxmox on ZFS, both GPUs in one container, layer split vs tensor split in llama.cpp, MTP, what 24 GB of VRAM unlocks (and where it stops), image and video generation across both cards with Raylight, and how to reach it from anywhere.

CHAPTERS
0:00 Can a second GPU double the speed?
0:52 The build (and the motherboard mistake)
2:51 The setup: Proxmox, ZFS, both GPUs in one container
6:22 Layer split vs tensor split
10:31 What 24 GB unlocks
12:32 Image and video: ComfyUI, then Raylight
14:42 Make it a server
16:25 Was it worth it?

THE RESULTS (everyday use, one card vs two)
- Qwen 3.6 35B MoE: ~70 → ~130 tok/s (154 on code prompts)
- Qwen 3.8 27B: ~14 → ~45 tok/s (55 on code), more than 3x, because one card had to push a third of the model to the CPU
- Full 262k context on the 35B, and vision on the GPU
- Qwen 3.8 Flash (125B + 50B Engram): bigger than both cards combined, so RAM is the upgrade there, not a second GPU
- MiniMax H3 video: ComfyUI uses one card; with Raylight both cards work, ~1:30 → 82 s per clip, RAM 52 GB → under 10 GB

HARDWARE
- AMD Ryzen 9 7900X (12 cores)
- 64 GB DDR5
- MSI MPG X870E Carbon WiFi (the non-MAX one: the second slot runs at x4)
- 2x RTX 3060 12 GB
- 1 TB NVMe

If you're buying a board for two GPUs, check the lane split in the manual's footnotes and aim for x8 / x8. Check what your cards actually get with:
nvidia-smi --query-gpu=index,name,pcie.link.gen.max,pcie.link.width.current --format=csv

THE LLAMA.CPP SETUP
Tensor split (both cards work on every layer):
llama-server -m Qwen3.8-27B-Q4_K_M.gguf -ngl 99 -fa on -c 122880 -sm tensor

Tensor split + MTP (the fast setup):
llama-server -m Qwen3.8-27B-GSQ-RCO-IQ3_S-mtp.gguf -ngl 99 -fa on -c 163840 -sm tensor -ctk q8_0 -ctv q8_0 --spec-type draft-mtp --spec-draft-n-max 2 --spec-draft-type-k q8_0 --spec-draft-type-v q8_0

Split ratios (GPU0 first): -ts 1,1 (even) · -ts 60,40 · -ts 35,65

LINKS
- llama.cpp tensor parallelism PR: https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/19378
- llama.cpp multi-GPU docs: https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/docs/multi-gpu.md
- Qwen 3.8 27B GSQ GGUF: https://huggingface.co/ISTA-DASLab/Qwen3.8-27B-GSQ-RCO-GGUF
- Raylight (multi-GPU ComfyUI): https://github.com/komikndr/raylight
- Arcane (Docker dashboard): https://github.com/getarcaneapp/arcane
- Nginx Proxy Manager: https://github.com/NginxProxyManager/nginx-proxy-manager
- Proxmox VE: https://www.proxmox.com/en/proxmox-virtual-environment
- Tailscale: https://tailscale.com

- Ryzen 9 7900X photo: CristoCalis, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikimedia Commons)

articles.title: Can You Run Any LLM in Jev Mode Using llama.cpp?
articles.author: Codacus
articles.summary: Jev answers in milliseconds, picks from your options instead of writing a paragraph, and you need a waitlist spot to try it. I added the same way of asking to llama.cpp, so it runs on the model already sitting on your drive and the card you already own. A new endpoint on llama-server takes your inst
articles.content:
Jev answers in milliseconds, picks from your options instead of writing a paragraph, and you
need a waitlist spot to try it. I added the same way of asking to llama.cpp, so it runs on the
model already sitting on your drive and the card you already own.

A new endpoint on llama-server takes your instructions, your schema and the current state, and
sends back every field with a value and a confidence score. Same server you use for chat, same
model in memory, one extra way to ask it things. On a 2 GB model in 2.4 GB of VRAM that is
17.3 ms per decision when you send them in bulk — and on the recorded demo in this video, 306 ms
against 3,415 ms for writing the same JSON, with all twelve fields identical.

None of this would exist without Harsha, who proved the idea in the open within hours of the
launch instead of keeping it to himself. His repo is below. All I did was carry it over to the
engine the rest of us already run.

So: which models love it, where it falls over, and what you would actually use it for.

⏱️ CHAPTERS
0:00 Intro
0:44 What Jev actually is
3:43 The secret sauce — choose instead of write
9:06 Jev mode in llama.cpp
13:15 Run it yourself — setup, start to finish
17:03 The model hunt: what it loves, what breaks it
20:59 What you'd actually use it for
25:01 What it comes down to

🔗 LINKS
Harsha's model (the original proof, Apache 2.0):
https://huggingface.co/harshatheg/Qwen-2.5-1B-RLCD
The llama.cpp branch with Jev mode:
https://github.com/thecodacus/llama.cpp/tree/parallel-decision
The decision playground:
https://github.com/thecodacus/decision-playground

🧰 WHAT'S IN THIS VIDEO
· A new `/v1/decision` endpoint on llama-server, and how it is wired
· Constrained choice instead of free text — one answer per field, plus a probability
· Scoring every option in parallel from one cached context
· 17.3 ms per decision in bulk on a 2 GB model, in 2.4 GB of VRAM
· Which models take to it: attention-only models fly, hybrids hit a batching wall
· Where it breaks, and what a wrong pick actually is (it is not a hallucination)
· A playground you can run against your own llama-server

❓ THE QUESTION
If you had a reflex like this wired into your own setup, what is the first job you would hand
it? I have got a list, and I will be sharing that journey with you all on this channel.

Making it respond fast took a lot more work. In this video, I build a local voice assistant inside Pithagoras and show each o
articles.content:
Try CodeRabbit : https://coderabbit.link/codacus-003

An Astra-like voice agent, running entirely on local hardware, with a 12GB GPU. But getting it to talk was the easy part. Making it respond fast took a lot more work.

In this video, I build a local voice assistant inside Pithagoras and show each optimization with real-time demos. We go from a slow, sequential pipeline to overlapping transcription, model generation, speech synthesis, and playback.

The agent can see screenshots, browse the web, use a terminal, and write documents in a live canvas, all through voice.

You’ll see:
• Why the original voice pipeline felt so slow
• Sentence chunking and parallel TTS generation/playback
• Transcribing while you’re still speaking
• Faster first replies while preserving thinking for follow-up work
• Breeze-TTS-2 quantization and streaming with audio.cpp

articles.content:
A 177-billion-parameter model, running on a five-year-old RTX 3060 with 12 GB of VRAM. Level with Claude Opus 4.8, going toe to toe with Opus 5 in a lab built specifically to trip it up — and not crawling.

The performance isn't even the crazy part. The crazy part is the architecture: a second "phrase book" of 51 billion parameters that isn't a neural network at all, it's a lookup table — and it can live on the SSD instead of the GPU. No open-weights lab has shipped this at frontier scale before.

In this video I explain how it works, get it running on real consumer hardware, benchmark every RAM size from 12 GB to 61 GB, and then put it through a three-task coding lab built to lie to the model — with tests that contradict the spec, decoy legacy files, and hidden checks the model never sees.

Hardware used:
RTX 3060 12 GB (used, ~$300)
Ryzen 5 5600X (6c/12t)
64 GB DDR4
3-bit quant,
82 GB model file.

The one setting to take away: thread count. 12 threads = 13.6 tok/s swinging wildly. 6 threads, one per real core = 24.4 tok/s and stable. ~50% over stock on the same card.
